sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Latent generative models typically rely on three separate networks: an encoder that tokenizes pixels, a generator that models the latent distribution, and a decoder that maps latents back to pixels. UNITE recently merged the first two into a single generative encoder trained in one stage, but its decoder remains a separate network. We ask whether this last network can be folded in too, so that one diffusion transformer encodes, generates, and decodes. Simply letting the shared backbone decode does not help. What makes it work is to cast all three modes as position-aligned sequence maps over one fully shared backbone, distinguished only by a mode token and the timestep. The resulting model, UNIFIED, is simple: one network trained from scratch in a single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, without adversarial losses or pretrained encoders (e.g., DINO). On ImageNet-1K 256x256 at matched parameters, UNIFIED improves gFID over UNITE at three sizes (~60M, ~115M, and ~215M) and reaches 2.08 with 215M parameters, the lowest among compared models under 250M parameters. On text-to-image generation, UNIFIED-B (218M) reaches a GenEval score of 0.87 at 512x512, exceeding single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters. Full unification of latent diffusion is thus not merely feasible but beneficial.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Latent diffusion models (Rombach et al., 2022; Peebles & Xie, 2023; Ma et al., 2024) rely on three trainable networks: an encoder that maps pixels to latents, generator that models the latent distribution, and decoder that maps latents back to pixels. They are usually trained in stages: the autoencoder is first trained for reconstruction, and then frozen while the generator is fit to its latents. This recipe fixes the representation before the model that must sample from it is trained. It also forces choice of how much capacity each network receives, and the effect of that choice on generation is hard to predict (Hansen-Estruch et al., 2025). We ask whether this pipeline can collapse into single diffusion transformer (DiT) whose every block is shared by encoding, denoising, and decoding, trained in single stage with only reconstruction loss and flow-matching loss, with no pretrained encoders such as DINO (Oquab et al., 2024). Most single-stage training methods keep the tokenizer and generator as separate networks (Vahdat et al., 2021; Leng et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026b; Heek et al., 2026), while the few that use single network still reserve parts of it for individual modes: LDMis-AE (Zhang et al., 2026) splits one DiT by depth into encoding and decoding blocks, which turns the allocation choice above into choice of split depth, and DSD (Wang & Zhang, 2025) adds dedicated diffusion head and relies on DINO alignment. UNITE (Duggal et al., 2026) is the closest step in this direction. It treats tokenization and generation as the same latent-inference problem and solves both with one generative encoder, trained in single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, but it still decodes pixels with separate network (Figure 2b). natural baseline is to let UNITEs backbone decode as well. We call this extension UNITE++ (Figure 2c): it shares every weight across the three modes and selects the mode with learned mode token. Like UNITE, it reads its outputs from readout tokens, which are extra input tokens whose outputs are taken as the latent or as pixels. We attribute this to the readout design: there is no direct mapping between latent tokens and image locations, so to decode, every image location must gather its content from the latent tokens through attention. We therefore propose UNIFIED (Figure 2d), single DiT that maps images to latents, latents to latents, and latents to images as position-aligned sequence maps: given sequence index refers to the same image location whether it holds pixel patch, latent, or noisy latent. The backbone is fully shared, and each mode is selected by learned mode token and lightweight input and output heads. Relative to UNITE, UNIFIED changes only the sequence layout, the timesteps for encoding and decoding, and the mode tokens, and replaces the standalone decoder with lightweight pixel output head. At 512 512, UNIFIED-B (218M) reaches 0.87 on GenEval and 0.827 on DPG-Bench, exceeding single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters (Section 4.5).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Our contributions are: We propose UNIFIED, single DiT that encodes, generates, and decodes with every backbone weight shared, trained from scratch in single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, without adversarial losses or pretrained encoders (e.g., DINO). We analyze how shared weights keep the three modes apart. We show that position alignment restores the reconstruction lost by naive full sharing, that the encoding timestep must match what the encoder reads, and that learned decoding timestep removes the conflict between decoding and generation at the clean endpoint, leading to better performance. At matched parameter counts on ImageNet, UNIFIED improves over UNITE at three parameter scales and attains the lowest gFID among compared models with at most 250M parameters. It also extends to text-to-image generation: at 512 512, UNIFIED-B (218M) exceeds single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Autoencoders and latent diffusion. Latent generative models typically follow two-stage recipe: an autoencoder is trained for reconstruction and frozen, and separate generator is then fit to its latents. The tokenizer is usually KL-regularized VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2014; Rezende et al., 2014) for latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022; Podell et al., 2024) or vector-quantized autoencoder (van den Oord et al., 2017; Razavi et al., 2019) for discrete generation, in both cases trained with the perceptual (Zhang et al., 2018) and adversarial losses popularized by VQGAN (Esser et al., 2021). Because the two stages are decoupled, progress has largely come one network at time: generators have moved to transformer backbones (Peebles & Xie, 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026b) and flow-based objectives (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023), while tokenizers have improved latent quantization (Mentzer et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024a) and compactness (Yu et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2025b). This decoupling has cost, however. The two stages optimize different objectives, which creates an optimization dilemma: latent that favors reconstruction can degrade generation. VA-VAE (Yao et al., 2025) addresses this dilemma by aligning the VAE latent with pretrained vision encoder (Caron et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024). Such encoders also serve as an alignment target for the generator (Yu et al., 2025), or even replace the tokenizers encoder in the latent diffusion pipeline (Zheng et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026). We instead revisit the recipe itself: single backbone serves as encoder, decoder, and generator, and is trained in single stage without relying on pretrained vision encoder. End-to-end tokenization and generation. Closer to our setting, several methods train the tokenizer and generator jointly (Leng et al., 2025; Duggal et al., 2026). The central difficulty is latent collapse: once the generation loss can shape the latent, the generator can lower its loss by making the latent trivial rather than modeling it (Leng et al., 2025; Wang & Zhang, 2025; Zheng et al., 2026b). Existing methods differ mainly in how they prevent this. Likelihood-based approaches keep variational bound whose KL or entropy terms hold the latent in place, and train score-based (Vahdat et al., 2021), normalizing-flow (Zhao et al., 2026), or diffusion (Zheng et al., 2026b; Heek et al., 2026) prior jointly with the autoencoder. REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025) instead anchors the latent to an external representation, backpropagating representation-alignment loss, rather than the diffusion loss, into the VAE. Other approaches stop the gradient through the denoising target and predict clean latents (Duggal et al., 2026; Wang & Zhang, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026); this needs neither variational bound nor an external encoder, and we adopt it. Closest to our work, three methods built on this recipe also share weights. UNITE (Duggal et al., 2026) merges the encoder and generator but keeps standalone decoder; LDM-is-AE (Zhang et al., 2026) splits one DiT by depth into encoding and decoding blocks, which requires manually choosing the split depth and the feature-mixing schedule; and DSD (Wang & Zhang, 2025) uses single ViT for all three modes with lightweight blocks for diffusion, but reintroduces an external alignment loss. UNIFIED instead shares every block of single DiT backbone across all three roles, with no role-specific blocks or alignment loss. Pixel diffusion. more direct way to avoid the two-stage recipe is to drop the latent and run diffusion on pixels. Early pixel-space models handle the high dimensionality with U-Net designs, adjusted noise schedules, and loss weightings (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021; Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Kingma & Gao, 2023; Hoogeboom et al., 2025), adaptive computation over small set of latent tokens (Jabri et al., 2023), or cascades across resolutions (Chen et al., 2025c). (d) UNIFIED (ours) removes all readout tokens: every pass maps same-length, position-aligned sequence (image x, noisy latent zt, or latent z) after mode token at position 0, and encodes clean images at tenc = 1 rather than 0. Follow-up works improve details with dedicated pixel-level modules (Yu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Ma et al., 2026a) or U-shaped skip connections (Guo et al., 2026), or draws on pretrained vision encoder for representation alignment (Shin et al., 2026), perceptual losses (Ma et al., 2026b), or denoising its features first (Baade et al., 2026). Likewise, UNIFIED trains one network in single stage, but keeps learned latent that the same backbone encodes and decodes. One transformer, many tasks. single transformer can serve many tasks when the task is specified through its input. The most common way is the input format: text prefix or prompt (Raffel et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2023; 2024a), the choice of input and target modalities (Mizrahi et al., 2023), in-context example pairs (Wang et al., 2023), or multimodal instruction (Xiao et al., 2025). Unified multimodal models (Chameleon Team, 2024; Zhou et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025) extend this to understanding and generation in one backbone. Another way is the corruption level of each input, set by per-modality or per-token timesteps (Bao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Le et al., 2025) or by masking ratios (Li et al., 2023; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2024): clean inputs act as conditions and heavily corrupted ones are generated, so one network can switch among conditional, joint, and marginal generation, or between representation learning and generation. In this paper, we use learned mode token and mode-specific timestep to direct single DiT backbone between tokenization and generation.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: UNIFIED replaces the encoder, generator, and decoder of latent diffusion with single diffusion transformer Tθ that operates in three modes: encoding, generation, and decoding. Each training step runs one pass per mode, and every pass is position-aligned sequence map, in which index refers to the same image location whether it holds pixel patch, latent token, or noised latent token. The backbone weights are fully shared; the modes differ only in lightweight input and output heads, in learned mode token prepended to the sequence, and in the AdaLN conditioning, namely the timestep and class label that is null outside generation  (Table 1)  .

sections.title: 3.3 SPECIFYING MODES IN SHARED WEIGHTS
sections.content: With every backbone weight shared, the three passes differ only in what enters the backbone: the values supplied by the input heads, the layout of the sequence, the mode token, and the conditioning (t, c). The class label is null in both encoding and decoding, so the layout, the mode token, and the timestep must keep the modes apart. We set each by single principle. Position alignment. In UNITE and UNITE++, the latent occupies its own group of readout tokens  (Table 1)  , so pixels and latents interact only through attention: encoding must route the content of every image location into latent readouts with no fixed spatial correspondence, and in UNITE++ decoding must route it back out to the pixel readouts. The backbone thus learns this routing on top of encoding and decoding themselves. UNIFIED instead aligns the sequences of all three modes: the pixel patch, latent token, and noised latent token share one sequence index and one RoPE position. This leaves attention to model context rather than to move content between pixels and latents. Alignment comes at cost. Readouts decouple the latent length from the number of patches, as in Perceiver-style readouts (Jaegle et al., 2022), while alignment ties = . In exchange, each encoding or decoding pass has length + 1 instead of 1 + + . Encoding timestep. The timestep is the backbones explicit signal of how much of the content at its output positions is observed: = 0 marks pure noise and = 1 clean latent. We set it in every mode to match that content. The generation pass reads zt and uses the sampled t. For the encoding pass, what the output positions hold depends on the layout. In UNITE and UNITE++, they hold (0, I) latent readouts, the same input from which sampling starts, so the matched choice is the noisy endpoint, tenc = 0: encoding is generation from noise, conditioned on the image through attention. Under position alignment, the same positions hold the observed image patches, so the matched choice becomes the clean endpoint, tenc = 1. Decoding timestep. Decoding reads clean latent, so the principle above would set tdec = 1. At the clean endpoint, however, the modes disagree on what to output: encoding and generation return the clean latent, whereas decoding returns pixels. The conflict is sharpest at the end of sampling. There the generation input zt enters through the same head in as the decoding input, and in the unconditional branch of classifier-free guidance both passes also carry the null label, so their AdaLN conditioning is identical and only the mode token, acting through attention, tells them apart. The conflict surfaces in the last blocks near = 1, where the two passes must diverge into different output spaces. We resolve it by conditioning decoding on its own learned embedding in place of the timestep embedding, denoted as tdec = 1 for timestep outside the flow interval.

sections.title: 4.1 FULL UNIFICATION IMPROVES GENERATION AT MATCHED SIZE
sections.content: Table 2 compares three ways of spending fixed parameter budget: separate networks, shared generative encoder with standalone decoder (UNITE), and one fully shared backbone (UNIFIED). Both UNIFIED variants improve gFID over UNITE at every size. The gain is largest when capacity is scarce (0.22 and 0.33 at Tiny and Small vs. 0.15 at Base), and Tiny UNIFIED nearly matches Small UNITE with about half the parameters (2.78 at 62M vs. 2.76 at 117M). This suggests that the shared backbone is more parameter-efficient than separate networks.

sections.title: 4.2 COMPARISON WITH PIXEL-SPACE AND LATENT DIFFUSION MODELS
sections.content: Table 4 compares UNIFIED with published class-conditional generators of at most 250M parameters on ImageNet-1K 256256. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented UNIFIED, single diffusion transformer that encodes, generates, and decodes with fully shared weights. We systematically study how to unify these modes, including partial versus full weight sharing, sequence layout, and the timestep conditioning of each mode, and find that it works best when the three modes are cast as position-aligned sequence maps and decoding receives its own learned timestep. At matched parameters on ImageNet-1K, UNIFIED improves generation over UNITE at every size. This also extends to text-to-image generation, where it is competitive with substantially larger models on GenEval, DPG-Bench, and GenAI-Bench, and at 512 512 exceeds single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters. Overall, full unification of latent diffusion is not merely feasible but beneficial.

sections.title: APPENDIX
sections.content: In this appendix, we first provide the ImageNet-1K training details and the evaluation protocols used across the paper. Then, we provide compute analysis on model training, the full comparison with pixel-space and latent diffusion models, and additional ablation results on ImageNet-1K. Next, we detail the text-to-image training and evaluation protocol and report zero-shot results on MSCOCO, and present results and implementation details for the QM9 molecule experiment. Finally, we discuss limitations. The last appendix shows uncurated ImageNet-1K samples.

sections.title: B IMAGENET EVALUATION PROTOCOLS
sections.content: We report Frechet FID computation. Inception Distance (FID) computed with the torch-fidelity library using InceptionV3 features. Reference statistics are computed over the full ImageNet-1K training set (1,281,167 images), and all FID scores are evaluated on 50K generated samples. Reconstruction metrics (rFID, rIS, PSNR, LPIPS) use the 50K ImageNet-1K validation images, center-cropped to 256 256 and passed through one encoding and one decoding pass with EMA weights.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Sampling protocol. Following UNITE (Duggal et al., 2026), we use class-balanced sampling, generating exactly 50 images for each of the 1,000 ImageNet classes (50K images in total). ODE solver. Every sample starts from Gaussian noise z0 (0, I) at = 0, and we integrate the probability flow ODE over the full interval [0, 1]. The main solver is the adaptive fifth-order DormandPrince solver (dopri5; absolute tolerance 106, relative tolerance 103), which chooses its own steps, so no time grid is involved. The velocity is obtained from the predicted clean latent as (ˆz zt)/(1 t), with the denominator clamped at 0.05. Classifier-free guidance. Following UNITE (Duggal et al., 2026), classifier-free guidance is applied only for [0.1, 1.0]; for < 0.1 the model is run without guidance. This interval restricts the guidance, not the integration, which always covers [0, 1]. We sweep the CFG scale ω from 1.0 to 4.0 in increments of 0.2 and report the best FID for each model. Protocol of each result. The protocol above produces every ImageNet-1K result in the paper (Tables 2, 3, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and the dopri5 columns of Table 14, and the training-budget panels of Figures 4 and 6), with two exceptions. (i) The early-termination experiment (Appendix E, Table 15) keeps dopri5 and the initial condition but ends the integration at tend < 1, at fixed CFG scale of 2.0. (ii) The sampling-budget panels of Figure 4 and the Euler columns of Table 14 replace dopri5 with fixed-step Euler solver over [0, 1]. With budget of NFE, it takes steps on the grid ti = αsi/(cid:0)1 + (α 1)si (cid:1), where si = i/K for = 0, . . . , and α = 0.5 is the noise-schedule shift used in training  (Table 7)  ; the grid is therefore denser near = 0. Each model uses the best CFG scale found with dopri5, and the guidance interval and the 50K class-balanced samples are unchanged. CKA analysis. We compare the backbones activations in the encoding and generation passes with linear CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019), using the debiased estimator (Song et al., 2012). For each validation image, we run the encoding pass on the image and the generation pass on its layernormalized latent noised to level (t = 1 is clean), both with the null class label; the noise is drawn once and reused at every t, so the curves differ only in t. We record each blocks output and keep only the positions that carry the latent: all positions for UNIFIED, and the readout positions for UNITE and UNITE++. For Separate, the two passes run in different networks, the encoder and the generator. CKA is computed within each image, with its tokens as samples, so it measures whether the two passes induce the same token-to-token similarity structure.

sections.title: C COMPUTE ANALYSIS
sections.content: UNIFIED reserves no parameters for any single mode, so training can assign the whole backbone to whichever task needs it, rather than fixing the split in advance as UNITEs encoder-to-decoder ratio does  (Table 11)  . We attribute its gFID gains at matched size to this (Table 2; Appendix E). The cost is compute: every mode runs the full backbone, whereas UNITE denoises with its generative encoder alone. Per step. At matched parameters (215M), the shared backbone is wider (984 vs. 768), so one flowmatching forward pass for UNIFIED costs 1.63 more than UNITE (81.7 vs. 50.1 GFLOPs). Per training step. The reconstruction branch costs about the same in both models (0.62 vs. 0.57 TFLOPs): UNIFIED encodes and decodes position-aligned 257-token sequences, while UNITE encodes 512 tokens of readouts and patches and decodes with separate decoder. Flow matching dominates the step (83% and 76% of compute), so full step for UNIFIED costs 1.50 more than UNITE (3.58 vs. 2.39 TFLOPs per image). At matched training compute. Training for the same number of epochs therefore gives UNIFIED 1.35, 1.72, and 1.50 the training compute of UNITE at Tiny, Small, and Base. Table 9 instead compares the two at matched total training FLOPs, using the UNIFIED checkpoints whose compute brackets UNITEs 200-epoch budget (the full curves are in Figures 4 and 6). Comparability. Results of other methods are taken from their papers and therefore differ in training length, sampler, and guidance settings. Our models are trained for 200 epochs, fewer than most baselines (600 for JiT and PixelREPA, and 4001600 for the two-stage models). UNITE is retrained under the same protocol as UNIFIED. Results. Among single-stage models of at most 220M parameters, UNIFIED attains the lowest gFID at every size: UNIFIED-T (62M, 2.78) already improves on all pixel-space baselines of 131 164M (2.963.66). sections.title: E ADDITIONAL ABLATION EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Decoder parameters are better spent in the shared backbone. At fixed Tiny budget  (Table 11)  , moving UNITEs capacity from the decoder to the encoder/generator improves gFID (1:2 1:1 2:1: 5.01 3.79 3.00), even though the decoder-heavy 1:2 reconstructs best. Removing the decoder altogether (UNIFIED) improves gFID further, to 2.78 (2.75 with tdec=1). Parameters thus help generation most when they sit in the shared backbone rather than in standalone decoder. Full results. Tables 11, 12, and 13 report every ImageNet-1K model at epoch 200, without and with CFG. Both UNIFIED variants improve on every UNITE allocation, as shown in Table 13. At Base, both UNIFIED variants reconstruct better than UNITE (lower rFID, higher rIS) at similar PSNR and LPIPS, while UNITE++ reconstructs worst. Moreover, encoding at tenc=0 instead of 1 hurts UNIFIED on both tasks (gFID 2.31 vs. 2.15, rFID 1.39 vs. 0.97), as shown in Table 12. The conclusions hold with and without guidance, and full unification costs reconstruction only at the smallest size. Variation across evaluation seeds. Every epoch-200 gFID and IS with CFG that we report for UNITE, UNITE++, and UNIFIED is the mean over repeated evaluations, and Table 14 gives these means with their standard deviations. Each seed draws different set of 50K initial noises; the checkpoint, class-balanced labels, and CFG scale are fixed. Every model is evaluated with five seeds. At Base, we repeat the evaluation with the adaptive dopri5 solver and with 256-step Euler solver (Appendix B). With dopri5, the standard deviation of gFID is at most 0.025, and the three ranges do not overlap: all five runs of UNIFIED (tdec=1) (2.0472.108) are below all five of UNIFIED (tdec=1) (2.1342.162), which are below all five of UNITE (2.2062.255). sections.title: H LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our evidence that full unification helps comes from images, where every sample shares one token grid that position alignment can exploit. On QM9 (Appendix G), where samples are unordered sets without such grid, UNIFIED generates as well as UNITE but reconstructs slightly worse. Whether this gap stems from limited decoding capacity at small scale or from position alignment itself, and how to adapt position alignment to such data, are left to future work. Our comparisons with UNITE are at 256 256. UNIFIED also works at 512 512 (Section 4.5), but whether its gains over separate decoder persist at higher resolutions and longer token sequences is left to future work. Full weight sharing also rules out freezing the latent space. With separate tokenizer, the latent space can be fixed, from the start or after joint training, and the generator trained alone on precomputed latents. In UNIFIED, every update to the shared backbone also changes the encoding and decoding passes, so the reconstruction objective must stay active throughout training, and each step pays for encoding and decoding passes alongside generation.
